cards.title: Graph Fundamentals
cards.teaser: A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) connected by edges. Edges can be directed (one-way) or undirected (two-way), and weighted (with a cost) or unweighted. Nearly every network, dependency, or relationship problem is secretly a graph.

runs.text: A
graph
G = (V, E) consists of a set of
vertices
V (also called nodes) and a set of
edges
E that connect pairs of vertices. Unlike trees, graphs have no hierarchy — any vertex can connect to any other, and cycles are allowed.
The two primary classifications are:

items.text: — edges have a direction: A → B does not imply B → A. Models Twitter follows, HTTP redirects, task dependencies.
— edges are bidirectional: if A connects to B, B connects to A. Models Facebook friendships, road maps, network cables.

runs.text: Edges may also carry a
weight
— a numeric cost like distance, latency, or price. Unweighted graphs treat all edges as equal cost (weight 1). The
degree
of a vertex is the count of edges incident to it; in directed graphs, in-degree and out-degree are tracked separately.

explanation.code:
# A directed, unweighted graph with 4 vertices and 5 edges
# Vertices: 0, 1, 2, 3
# Edges (directed): 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3, 3→0

# Key vocabulary
# path      — sequence of vertices where consecutive pairs are connected by edges
# cycle     — a path that starts and ends at the same vertex
# connected — every vertex is reachable from every other (undirected)
# DAG       — Directed Acyclic Graph: directed, no cycles; used for task scheduling

runs.text: Recognizing when a problem is a graph is the first skill. Explicit clues: 'network', 'dependency', 'route'. Implicit clues: state transitions (each state is a vertex), word ladders (each word is a vertex), or any problem where you model 'things and relationships between things'.

A graph is just dots (vertices) connected by lines (edges). The lines can have arrows (directed) or not (undirected), and they can carry numbers representing cost (weighted) or not. Almost any 'things connected to other things' problem — maps, dependencies, social networks — is a graph in disguise.

cards.title: Adjacency List Representation
cards.teaser: An adjacency list stores a graph as a dictionary mapping each vertex to its list of neighbors. Space is O(V + E) — proportional to what actually exists. It's the default choice for sparse graphs where most vertices have few connections.

runs.text: The
adjacency list
is the most common graph representation. Each vertex maps to a collection of its neighbors. In Python, a
dict[vertex, list[vertex]]
works perfectly for unweighted graphs; for weighted graphs, store tuples
(neighbor, weight)

explanation.code:
from collections import defaultdict

# Undirected, unweighted graph
graph: dict[str, list[str]] = defaultdict(list)

def add_edge(u: str, v: str) -> None:
    graph[u].append(v)
    graph[v].append(u)   # remove this line for directed graph

add_edge('A', 'B')
add_edge('A', 'C')
add_edge('B', 'D')
add_edge('C', 'D')

print(dict(graph))
# {'A': ['B', 'C'], 'B': ['A', 'D'], 'C': ['A', 'D'], 'D': ['B', 'C']}

# Weighted directed graph
weighted: dict[str, list[tuple[str, int]]] = defaultdict(list)
weighted['A'].append(('B', 4))
weighted['A'].append(('C', 2))

runs.text: Complexity analysis:

items.text: — one entry per vertex plus one slot per edge. For a sparse graph with millions of nodes but few edges per node, this is vastly more efficient than a matrix.
— to check if edge (u, v) exists, scan u's neighbor list. Slow for dense graphs; fast for sparse ones.
— the core operation of BFS and DFS. Natural and efficient with a list.

runs.text: Use a set instead of a list for neighbors when you need O(1) edge-existence checks and don't care about order: graph[u] = set(). This trades slightly more memory for faster 'is (u, v) an edge?' queries.

An adjacency list is a dictionary where each key is a vertex and its value is a list of neighbors. It only stores connections that actually exist, so it's memory-efficient when most pairs of vertices aren't connected. Building and iterating is fast; checking a specific edge is slow.

cards.title: Adjacency Matrix Representation
cards.teaser: An adjacency matrix is a V×V grid where cell [i][j] = 1 (or the weight) if edge (i, j) exists, and 0 otherwise. Edge lookup is O(1), but space is O(V²) — only practical when the graph is dense.

runs.text: An
adjacency matrix
represents a graph as a two-dimensional array
matrix[V][V]
. If vertices are indexed 0 to V-1, then
matrix[i][j] = 1
means edge (i, j) exists. For weighted graphs, store the weight instead of 1, and use 0 or
float('inf')
to represent missing edges.

explanation.code:
# 4-vertex undirected graph using an adjacency matrix
V = 4
matrix = [[0] * V for _ in range(V)]

def add_edge(u: int, v: int, weight: int = 1) -> None:
    matrix[u][v] = weight
    matrix[v][u] = weight   # remove for directed graph

add_edge(0, 1)
add_edge(0, 2)
add_edge(1, 3)
add_edge(2, 3)

# matrix:
# [0, 1, 1, 0]   vertex 0 connects to 1 and 2
# [1, 0, 0, 1]   vertex 1 connects to 0 and 3
# [1, 0, 0, 1]   vertex 2 connects to 0 and 3
# [0, 1, 1, 0]   vertex 3 connects to 1 and 2

# O(1) edge check
print(matrix[0][1])  # 1  (edge exists)
print(matrix[0][3])  # 0  (no edge)

runs.text: Complexity analysis:

items.text: — always. A graph with 10,000 vertices needs a 100-million-cell matrix regardless of edge count.
— direct index access. This is the matrix's primary advantage over adjacency lists.
— must scan the entire row to find all neighbors, even if the vertex has only 2 edges.

runs.text: Avoid adjacency matrices for sparse graphs. A social network with 1 billion users and an average of 300 friends has E ≈ 300B edges vs V² = 10^18 matrix cells — the matrix would be astronomically wasteful.

An adjacency matrix is a spreadsheet where rows and columns are vertices. Put a 1 (or weight) where an edge exists, 0 elsewhere. Checking any edge is instant — just look up the cell. The cost is space: you always allocate V×V cells, most of which are 0 in sparse graphs.

cards.title: Sparse vs Dense Graphs
cards.teaser: A sparse graph has far fewer edges than the maximum possible (E << V²). A dense graph has edges approaching V². Adjacency lists win on sparse graphs; adjacency matrices win on dense ones — and the crossover is typically E ≈ V²/log V.

runs.text: The maximum possible number of edges in an undirected graph with V vertices is
— about V². A
sparse graph
has E much smaller than V² (e.g., road networks, social graphs, dependency DAGs). A
dense graph
has E approaching V² (e.g., complete graphs, fully connected neural layers, correlation matrices).
The choice of representation affects algorithm performance:

items.text: — O(V + E). With adjacency matrix — O(V²). For a sparse graph where E ≈ V, the list version is O(V) while the matrix version is always O(V²).
— inherently O(V³), so the O(V²) space of a matrix is acceptable. Works naturally with matrices.
— O((V + E) log V) with a list, vs O(V² log V) with a matrix. List wins decisively for sparse graphs.

explanation.code:
# Quick heuristic: compare E to V²
V, E = 1_000, 5_000

density = E / (V * (V - 1) / 2)
print(f"Density: {density:.4f}")  # 0.010 — very sparse, use adjacency list

V2, E2 = 100, 8_000
density2 = E2 / (V2 * (V2 - 1) / 2)
print(f"Density: {density2:.4f}")  # 1.621 — nearly complete, use matrix

runs.text: Rule of thumb: if average degree (E/V) is a small constant (like 3–10), the graph is sparse — use adjacency list. If E is comparable to V², use matrix. In practice, almost all real-world graphs (web, social, maps) are sparse.

Sparse means most pairs of vertices are not connected (a city road map). Dense means most pairs are connected (a tournament bracket where everyone plays everyone). Sparse graphs prefer adjacency lists to avoid allocating a huge mostly-empty matrix. Dense graphs can afford the matrix and benefit from its O(1) edge lookups.

cards.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
cards.teaser: BFS explores a graph level by level using a queue. It visits all neighbors of the current vertex before moving deeper, guaranteeing that the first time it reaches a vertex is via the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph.

runs.text: Breadth-First Search starts at a source vertex and explores outward in rings — all vertices at distance 1 first, then distance 2, and so on. A
visited
set prevents revisiting vertices (and infinite loops on cyclic graphs). The queue is what enforces level-by-level ordering: enqueue neighbors, then dequeue and process.
Time: O(V + E) — each vertex is enqueued once, each edge is inspected once. Space: O(V) for the queue and visited set.

BFS is the right tool whenever you want the shortest path in an unweighted graph, or need to process vertices in distance order from a source. It also solves: word ladders, minimum knight moves on a chessboard, and multi-source BFS (start with multiple sources simultaneously by seeding the queue with all of them).

BFS is like ripples in a pond. You drop a stone at the source — that's level 0. All nodes one hop away light up next — level 1. Then their unvisited neighbors — level 2. A queue keeps you processing in this order. Because BFS reaches each node via the fewest hops possible, the first path it finds is always the shortest (by edge count).

cards.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
cards.teaser: DFS dives as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking. Implemented with a stack (explicit or via recursion), it's the foundation for cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, and maze solving.

runs.text: Depth-First Search picks a vertex, follows one unvisited neighbor as far as possible, then backtracks to try the next option. Recursion naturally supplies the stack; for large graphs, an explicit stack avoids Python's recursion limit.
Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V) for the stack and visited set. The key behavioral difference from BFS: DFS explores one complete path to its end before trying another, while BFS fans out evenly.

The mnemonic: BFS uses a Queue (first in, first out — explore in order of discovery). DFS uses a Stack (last in, first out — always chase the newest frontier). Swap the deque for a list in the BFS template and you get DFS.

DFS is like exploring a maze by always choosing a path and walking it to the bitter end before backtracking. A stack (or recursion) keeps track of where you've been. It doesn't find the shortest path, but it visits every vertex and edge, making it the right tool for detecting cycles, finding connected components, and building topological orderings.

cards.title: Cycle Detection with DFS Coloring
cards.teaser: DFS-based cycle detection assigns each vertex one of three colors: white (unvisited), gray (in the current DFS path), and black (fully processed). Finding a gray neighbor during DFS means you've found a back edge — a cycle.

runs.text: In a directed graph, a cycle exists when DFS encounters a
back edge
— an edge to an ancestor in the current DFS recursion stack. The three-coloring scheme makes this detectable:

items.text: — vertex is on the current DFS call stack (being processed).
— vertex fully processed; all descendants explored.

runs.text: The gray node test is what separates cycle detection from plain DFS. A black neighbor means 'been there, done that' — safe. A gray neighbor means 'still on our current path' — cycle. This insight directly enables topological sort: if no gray neighbors are ever found, a valid ordering exists.

Think of DFS as painting vertices as you go. When you first visit a vertex, paint it gray (in progress). When you finish exploring all its descendants, paint it black (done). If during DFS you ever see a gray neighbor, you've looped back to something still on your current path — that's a cycle. Black neighbors are safe; gray ones are not.

cards.title: Topological Sort
cards.teaser: Topological sort orders vertices of a DAG so every edge points from earlier to later. Kahn's algorithm uses in-degree counting and a queue (BFS-based). DFS-based sort appends vertices in reverse finish order. Both run in O(V + E).

runs.text: A
topological ordering

of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) lists vertices such that for every edge u → v, u appears before v. This is undefined if the graph has a cycle. Applications: build systems (compile order), task schedulers, package dependency resolution, spreadsheet recalculation.

Kahn's algorithm has a cycle-detection bonus: if the result list is shorter than the total vertex count, some vertices were never enqueued — meaning they were stuck in a cycle with in-degree never reaching zero. DFS-based sort requires separate cycle detection.

Topological sort answers: 'given tasks with prerequisites, in what order should I run them?' Kahn's approach is intuitive — repeatedly pick any task with no remaining prerequisites, schedule it, and remove its edges. DFS-based sort does a full traversal and appends each vertex only after all its descendants are scheduled, then reverses the result.

cards.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
cards.teaser: Dijkstra's finds the shortest path from a source to all vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It greedily extracts the minimum-distance unvisited vertex using a min-heap, running in O((V + E) log V).

runs.text: Dijkstra's algorithm maintains a distance table initialized to infinity for all vertices except the source (distance 0). A min-heap priority queue always gives the next unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance. When a vertex is extracted, its shortest distance is finalized — the greedy step that makes this correct for non-negative weights.

Why it fails with negative weights: once a vertex's distance is finalized by extraction from the heap, Dijkstra assumes no shorter path can exist. A negative edge arriving later could produce a shorter path, but the algorithm has already moved on. Use Bellman-Ford when negative weights are possible.

The 'stale entry' check (if d > dist[u]: continue) is critical when using Python's heapq, which has no decrease-key operation. Instead, push a new (distance, vertex) entry and skip it if a shorter path has already been found.

Dijkstra is GPS routing in algorithm form. Start at source with distance 0, everything else is infinity. Repeatedly pick the closest unfinalized vertex, lock in its distance, and update neighbors if going through it is cheaper. A min-heap makes the 'pick closest' step fast. It only works when all road distances are positive — one negative shortcut breaks the greedy guarantee.

cards.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
cards.teaser: Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths from a source even when edges have negative weights. It relaxes all edges V-1 times in O(VE) time, and a final pass detects negative-weight cycles — something Dijkstra cannot do.

runs.text: Bellman-Ford works by
relaxation
: for each edge (u, v, w), if
dist[u] + w < dist[v]
, update
dist[v]
. The key insight: the shortest path in a graph with V vertices contains at most V-1 edges (no repeated vertices). After V-1 full passes over all edges, all shortest paths are correctly computed.

items.text: — V-1 iterations, each scanning all E edges. Slower than Dijkstra but handles negatives.
— if the V-th relaxation pass still updates any distance, a negative cycle exists (infinite loop of decreasing cost).

runs.text: Bellman-Ford is used in distance-vector routing protocols (RIP). Each router iteratively tells neighbors its best-known distances, equivalent to one Bellman-Ford relaxation round. Negative cycles in routing would cause routing loops, which is why RIP uses hop-count limits.

Bellman-Ford is the patient version of shortest-path. It goes through every edge in the graph, over and over, V-1 times — updating distances whenever a shorter route is found. Because it doesn't commit greedily like Dijkstra, it handles negative edges. A bonus final pass reveals negative cycles: if a distance still improves, you're stuck in an infinite cost-reducing loop.

cards.title: Minimum Spanning Tree: Kruskal's and Prim's
cards.teaser: A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) connects all vertices of an undirected weighted graph with the minimum total edge weight and no cycles. Kruskal's sorts edges and uses Union-Find; Prim's grows the MST greedily from a seed vertex using a priority queue.

runs.text: A
spanning tree
of a connected graph G is a subgraph that includes all V vertices with exactly V-1 edges and no cycles. The
Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
is the spanning tree with the smallest total edge weight. Applications: network cable layout, cluster analysis, approximation algorithms for TSP.

items.text: — dominated by sorting. Better for sparse graphs. Naturally parallelizable.
— with a min-heap. Better for dense graphs or adjacency matrix input.

runs.text: Both algorithms are greedy and both produce a correct MST — the greedy-choice property holds because the cut property guarantees: for any cut of the graph, the minimum-weight crossing edge is always in some MST.

The MST problem: connect all cities with cable at minimum total cost, with no redundant loops. Kruskal's is bottom-up — sort all cables by cost, keep adding the cheapest one that doesn't create a loop (Union-Find enforces this). Prim's is top-down — start at one city, always extend to the cheapest reachable unconnected city. Both guarantee the globally cheapest network.

cards.title: Connected Components and Union-Find
cards.teaser: Connected components partition an undirected graph into groups where every vertex can reach every other. Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) tracks these groups in nearly O(1) per operation using path compression and union by rank.

runs.text: A
connected component

is a maximal subgraph where every pair of vertices is connected by a path. An undirected graph with V vertices and C components has exactly C groups. Finding all components with DFS/BFS is O(V + E) — run a traversal from each unvisited vertex.
For dynamic connectivity — where edges are added one at a time —
Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union, DSU)
is far more efficient than re-running BFS/DFS. Two optimizations make it near-constant time:
path compression
(flatten the tree during find) and
union by rank
(attach the smaller tree under the larger). Together they yield amortized O(α(V)) per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively O(1).

Union-Find is the engine behind Kruskal's MST algorithm, network connectivity checks, and LeetCode 'number of islands' variants. Any time you need to dynamically merge groups and query 'are X and Y in the same group?', Union-Find is the right data structure.

Union-Find is a data structure that tracks which items are in the same group, and merges groups efficiently. Each item starts as its own group. union(x, y) merges x's group with y's group. find(x) returns x's group ID. Path compression makes the tree flat over time so find is nearly instantaneous. It's the go-to tool whenever you're building up connected groups one link at a time.
